records.title: Show HN: Pgxio – a tiny PostgreSQL layer inside Nginx
records.author: hito
records.storyText:
I built the first version of this stuff a decade ago as ethanolus (c2h5oh). And I've used it for most of my projects as a backend layer since then.

The main motive is to eliminate unnecessary complexity from backend layers.

How it works: a rust nginx module calls postgresql functions via non-blocking libpq io. There is an optional patch for libpq. It provides zero-copy for nginx-chained memory buffers - to avoid request body copies between nginx and libpq.

Pgxio supports http2 and websockets. Realtime listen/notify updates from postgres without polling.

How to try - code on github. Tested on Debian - FreeBSD validation in progress.

It's alpha - so any feedback is welcome.

records.title: Show HN: FELF – AppImage-like single binaries without FUSE, root, or a runtime
records.author: Rucadi
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

I've always had a bad time redistributing programs that use shared libraries, AppImage in my opinion does too much, and a container is an overkill - not always integrates smoothly.

I've moved to nix since long ago, but redistributing between nix and other distros or vice versa it's still a pain in the ass, more so if you want to run an alien app in nix or a nix app without the package manger in any other distro.

For that, with the help of Claude, I've implemented a format that deduces at pack-time all the shared libraries a program needs, puts them, together with its own glibc and a patched dynamic linker into a single executable.

This means that you don't actually need a runtime nor any special capability, it can run inside a FROM SCRATCH docker, alpine linux etc... And it also supports coreutils-like multiple programs accessible via symlinks, so it is a good fit for that purpose.

You can just use:

> felf pack $(which git) --output git.felf

and you'll have already a git binary that works everywhere, no matter which distro you are building this from. This only packs the binary and their dependencies.

Essentially, the effect is similar as if you LD_PRELOAD's all the libraries that it requires.

In the end, we have been fighting these demons since long long ago, chroots/docker/appimage/flatpack/nix etc...

So this xkcd applies: https://xkcd.com/927/

I'm happy to share the project, I hope it inspires new discoveries/tools in this regard!

records.title: Show HN: My first project, an AI-powered financial news analyzer
records.author: lamarcol
records.storyText:
I'm 17, and I started NotBot a few months ago to see whether I could turn an idea into a working project. My main interest is economics, not becoming a programmer, but I enjoy experimenting with code.

A few months ago, I had the idea of creating a program that would analyze the most recent news about a specific stock and calculate a weighted average of their polarity to create a sort of sentiment indicator.

While researching, I found a YouTube video about creating a simple GitHub repository that did, in a simplified and imprecise way, what I had in mind. At first glance, I realized it was a very simple program: feedparser retrieved news from Google News, beautifulsoup4 extracted the content, the sentiment was analyzed with FinBERT, running through Transformers and PyTorch.

From there, I started modifying it with the free versions of Gemini. I had to solve a lot of problems, for example fixing the extraction of articles from Google News, I managed to solve it with a new library (googlenewsdecoder).

Then I had to replace FinBERT, because it classified sentiment based on the context of the words but didn't take into account the actual impact of the event using external sources.

I experimented with an LLM that allowed me to specify the evaluation criteria more precisely through a prompt. I found a free one with rather strict TPM and RPM limits (it was called openai/gpt-oss-120b).

I also created two coefficients: one that adjusted the reliability of the news based on its source, and another that adjusted its impact based on how recent it was (all selected news articles had been published within the last 24 hours). Each article was divided into title, description, and content, and each of these three sections had a different weight based on predefined values (title 35%, description 25%, and text 40%). If the content had fewer than 100 characters, the text was not assigned any weight, and the title accounted for 60% while the description accounted for 40%.

After these modifications, I took a break of about a month because of school commitments, during which I discovered Codex (OpenAI's agent).

I changed the main LLM and implemented Gemini (3.1 Flash-Lite) because the TPM limits of the LLM I was using were too restrictive.

Even though I started using Gemini, I didn't discard Groq. In fact, I used it as a fallback in case Gemini returned some kind of error.

Another important modification was the addition of asynchronous article downloading through aiohttp and the processing of multiple articles simultaneously through asyncio. Later, I decided to start using Groq again for article analysis. In fact, I had both LLMs analyze the longer articles and then calculated the average of their two polarity scores.

The first was Finnhub, which allowed me to search for many more news articles about a specific stock (by entering its name and ticker).

At that point, I had to split up the code because the script had become very long.

The last modification I made concerned news selection: I implemented a filter that prevented similar news articles from being selected, to avoid excessively distorting the polarity in an incorrect way.

First of all, I'd like to know, from an expert, how well the project is built from a structural point of view and how it could be improved. For future projects, what parameters should I take into consideration to understand whether a project is well built?

Secondly, I'd like to know how I can determine whether a program like this can actually work, or at least how it could be useful (even with some modifications).

The third and final point is: which aspects of the pipeline might require more attention or could be optimized? Does it make sense to continue working on the project (also with the idea of turning it into a product), or am I approaching a structural limit?

records.title: Show HN: MyBox – Isolate your projects in a Linux box
records.author: janpmz
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I’ve built MyBox to isolate my development projects in Linux containers.

Installing npm modules on my machine didn’t feel right anymore.

MyBox is built on a fork of apple/container.

- Each box has its own Linux kernel.

- Project files get copied into the box (no folder mounts).

- Packet filtering blocks access to the Mac and local network (internet access from the box is allowed).

- Mac apps cannot reach into the box (a dedicated macOS account owns the runtime and virtual disks).

- Touch ID or a password is required to access the box (e.g. opening a shell, importing & exporting files).

I started with a CLI tool, but for convenience I’ve built a desktop app around it.

https://github.com/janpmz/mybox

records.title: Show HN: Airlock – Policy-as-code for fleets of AI coding agents
records.author: lovetocode
records.storyText:
My name is Matt and I am building Airlock. Airlock is going to be an open standard on managing autonomous fleets of engineering agents. I am seeking constructive feedback on the direction of this project and also asking what are your major pain points with managing AI use at larger businesses. Right now I am running my own company using this framework with a total of 23 workflows across four large scale projects.

Airlock is still really early, only 3-4 weeks old.

Airlock's configuration standard is aimed to be open source and I will also open source the backplane once I gain a bit more confidence in what I have built here and it is a bit more ready for public scrutiny. Today the schema itself and the reusable GitHub actions are publicly available. I will selfishly figure out how to monetize this at some point but my desired customer is going to be larger enterprises. Airlock kind of does a lot of things but if I had to sum it up in several bullet points it would be:

1) Allows for the configuration of agent behaviors and life cycles under version control. Each agent run proves who it is with GitHub’s OIDC token, and Airlock trades that for a GitHub token that lasts one hour and can only touch the repos and permissions listed in that agent’s role file.

2) Allows for configuring levels of autonomy starting with a repository's base autonomy level with stricter overrides down to individual files within a code base. (e.g. you trust agents for most of the repo but perhaps you want extra gating around the 'billing' or 'auth' modules).

3) Supports a standard autonomy scale. At level 4 agents are leading a project's direction while at level 1 they are dependent on humans to lead the direction of a project.

4) Provides an out-of-the-box OTEL collector that stores a subset of agent actions you would care about in the event of an audit. I’m exploring storing agent prompts and user prompts so that only the customer can decrypt them, and haven’t decided how.

5) Comes with a shadow mode that allows you to run Airlock and observe how it would behave in your org without turning it on.

To try it you just need to install the GitHub App, create a policy repository and run on GitHub hosted runners. I personally use self-hosted runners on EC2 spot instances. Visit https://airlock.lunareng.com/docs/quickstart to get started.

I have been really passionate lately about exploring how businesses of the [near] future will effectively manage autonomous development using agents at scale. I want to help answer the question of how can the business better manage AI spend, prioritization of token usage, auditability of agent actions and compliance with various governance, risk and compliance frameworks.

I am coming from the perspective of being an engineer for 15+ years but I have somehow managed to also develop a good understanding of how larger businesses operate. My vision of the future looks like a world where engineers don't use agent harnesses directly from their computer [for coding]. Instead engineering teams are managing a larger backlog of work that is automatically picked up by these agents. Engineering will instead be less about writing code and more about effectively deploying technology to solve business problems.

Thanks for taking a look and I look forward to meeting you in the comments.

References: https://github.com/lunareng/airlock-actions https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/role.schema.json https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/autonomy.schema.json https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/config.schema.json https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-dev... https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutori...

records.title: Show HN: TimeScroll – an open-source, local replacement for Rewind on Mac
records.author: XInTheDark
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I've been building TimeScroll since September 2025. It's a Mac app that records your screen in the background, so you can scroll back through your day or search for anything you've seen. It is local and open-source. The key features are introduced on the site, so I'll try to reduce the repetition in this post.

My motivation for building was (1) Rewind shutting down and the lack of alternatives that are as polished and direct; (2) Most apps like this (including Rewind really) are super CPU and storage intensive, to the point of having a noticeable impact on your battery life.

I identified a few issues with the 'standard' way of capturing and made it a point to fix them in this app.

1. The part I spent the most time on is how the text gets captured. Basically all the apps run OCR on every screenshot, which means the heavy OCR step will always take a certain amount of CPU. I noticed that the text is already inside the apps, so I took the completely different approach of reading it through the macOS Accessibility API instead (which I call Direct mode). It has big advantages - gets the exact text with no misread characters, along with the position of each line, and it's much cheaper than OCR.

The problem was that Chrome and Electron apps don't work very well with it, as they wouldn't create an accessibility tree unless requested, so I needed to set AXManualAccessibility attribute. Also, the text can be buried under many layers of the tree, so I have to write logic to traverse the tree within a time limit and capture as much useful text as possible. I haven't seen any screen capture app do these, so I had to figure most of it out on my own.

There are also a lot of implementation details - like first computing which windows are on each display and which parts of them are visible on screen. Ultimately, my measurements were around 9ms of CPU time to read a frame initially, but on subsequent reads, it can go as low as 0.4 ms.

The newest feature is summaries. You can select any range on the timeline and get your time in each app plus a written summary from a local model through Ollama. The main implementation trick used in the summary is (1) dividing the usage into 'sessions' using heuristics and (2) using the existing embeddings (from AI search) to choose a few representative screens to pass to the model.

2. Storage optimizations. I chose HEVC video to store the snapshots with one "segment" file per minute. The encoding process was something I needed to tune over time. Currently, I am using a constant quality setting with one keyframe per segment. On text-heavy frames, the approach I used managed to reduce it from 84 KB per frame to 20 KB, at slightly better quality.

There is also a lot of duplicate text that would multiply the storage use if stored for each snapshot, so deduplication and compression were huge things to figure out. Needless to say, all of this took many tries to get right, especially working with extracting/storing frames to the video files efficiently.

The end result is that TimeScroll uses ~2GB/month with normal daily usage and averages 1.1% CPU and 150-250MB memory on an M4 over a few days of normal use, whereas an older post about Rewind I found measured it to be "200MB/hour" and 20% CPU, which is ... a lot in comparison.

There are a lot of other things and approaches I tried that I can't fit here, but anyways, I'd really like feedback, especially on Direct mode and on the newer features - hope you enjoy the app!

records.title: Show HN: Product Analytics for your agent. 100x+ cheaper analytics/BI
records.author: Jonovono
records.storyText:
Hey all, a little while ago I set up Openpanel in some of my projects but very quickly hit the limits and was starting to have to pay $50 to keep the events flowing in. I thought this was crazy, as I really wasnt sending that many events.

I was thinking, surely it can't be that expensive to store events. I looked into self hosting Openpanel, and it's even crazier. You need redis, clickhouse, postgres, beefy machine. I realized I am paying a tonne of money for features that are completely irrelevent now. I don't need instant charts. In fact, I would prefer to never even go to your ugly dashboard and figure out how to use it. So i'm paying this extreme premium so these services can compute all these indexes and what not so they can deliver me any chart I want in a second. It's crazy.

I thought about what I really needed as a lot of my work is done with claude/codex now and realized all I really wanted was to get the raw events and have my agent analyze them with duckdb, let me ask questions, and make charts.

I looked at a few ways of doing this but the simplest and cheapest was cloudflare. Literally, just store the events in R2, and then the agent can pull them down when it wants.

What I do instead is I have a 1tb SSD, I pull down my events from r2 when I want and load it into duckdb. Now my agent can do whatever it wants. It's not limited by the capabilities gifted to me by amplitude etc. Heck, it can even write python scripts or anything. You could create Jupyter notebooks to view it, so many options.

I have been using this in prod, but thought i'd open it up if anyone wants to try: https://slurp.run/

It's fully open source, and you can one click to install it. Lmk if you try it and run into any issues.

One cool thing I got working too, is you can literally point your segment/sentry clients at the cloudflare endpoint.

I'm a college student, and I enjoy playing word games like Codenames, but it can be hard sometimes to find enough people to play when everyone is available, so I made an app that allows you to fill any seat with an AI teammate and also play against AI. This way it allows for people to get the full strategic experience of codenames just on their own.

Through this experiment, I was also able to measure and benchmark a few different LLMs through AWS Bedrock API calls and give them ELO ratings based on stuff like win rate and clue/guess accuracy. If anyone is interested, they can see more about my benchmarking methodology here: https://wordspies.com/hn#method. I think it's pretty interesting because it gives you a lot of insight into these various LLMs' NLP capabilities.

A few interesting stats were that I rated Gemini 4 Argon at 1775, GPT-6.1 Sol at 1744, GPT-6 Astra at 1723, Claude Fable 5.1 at 1623, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 1592. You'll find a few interesting things there, like how, although newer, more expensive models tend to perform better, some rare exceptions exist, like Kimi K2.5 slightly edging out Kimi K3.

Check out the site if you're interested in NLP and data science and want to see what level of frontier LLMs you can beat!

records.title: Show HN: Search Everywhere at Once. Instantly
records.author: civnode
records.storyText:
I've made AntiFind, to allow you to search everywhere at once, vastly increasing the efficiency of LLMs and your own searches:

AntiFind indexes filesystems, not folders.

It maintains a live view of storage by reading filesystem metadata directly. Because it understands the underlying filesystems, it can search across storage that the operating system is not currently exposing, including unmounted partitions.

Allowing you to search for and play media from Linux in your Windows and the other way around. Without mounting the drives.

This works on Linux, Windows and MacOS.

The underlying idea is simple: instead of walking directories, read the filesystem's file tables directly.

Most tools discover the filesystem again every time you search. AntiFind reads the drive's metadata in one pass and then follows changes as they happen.

AntiFind supports Windows, Linux and macOS. It includes both a GUI and a command line. The CLI supports JSON output (--json) and was designed to integrate cleanly with automation and LLM workflows.

There's a lot more to it, and you can find timings on my site, but that's the core idea.

More information: https://antisoftworks.com/antifind

Cheers!

records.title: Show HN: Native Tcl/Tk Wayland and Android Port
records.author: wusspuss
records.storyText:
Native Wayland for Tk was proposed years ago as a hard GSoC project ( https://wiki.tcl-lang.org/page/GSoC+Idea%3A+Tk+Backend+for+t... ) - and let's be honest, it's very hard for humans. Turns out AI cracks it in a few hours.

Claude was given the freedom to make its choices from top to bottom, including stack and architecture. It came up with a thin X11 emulation layer, the same approach Tk's macOS and Windows ports already take - except this one is shared by Wayland and Android thanks to their similarity. The human in the loop merely tested and sanity-checked the outcome to her unexpected satisfaction. Tkabber (a large, long-lived XMPP client) runs on the Wayland port unaltered, and on Android with one small fix.

Unlike AndroWish (an SDL-based Tcl/Tk distribution for Android), this is a backend inside Tk itself, shared with the Wayland port: Cairo/HarfBuzz drawing, with touch and the on-screen keyboard handled in generic Tk through new commands and events.

If you want to experience an anachronism, you can try the APK of the Tk demo with an added multitouch example ( https://github.com/pounceandmiss/tk-wayland/releases/ ), and full-on Tkabber on Android ( https://github.com/pounceandmiss/tkabber-demo/releases/ ).

records.title: Show HN: slcc, a C compiler that doesn't need semicolons or braces
records.author: itzmetanjim
records.storyText:
hi, i made this mostly as a joke. it started when i found that replacing (almost) all skip(';') in tcc with if(tok==';') skip(';') essentially adds some highly basic auto semicolon insertion. then i expanded on the idea and kept adding more stuff and fixing up the semicolon stuff a bit and added python style indentation.

so now it's a fork of tcc (fabrice bellard's tiny c compiler) where semicolons are optional and you can use indentation instead of braces, so you can write stuff like

    int main():
        printf("hello\n")
        return 0
its not just at the end of lines by the way

    int a, b float c // a semicolon is inserted between b and float
    for (int i=1 i <= 5 i++): // ... or between statements
        printf("%d ", i)
the indentation part is just a pass before lexing that turns lines ending in "):" or "else:" into "{" and adds the closing "}" when the indentation drops.

the obvious problem is that without semicolons a statement just keeps going as long as the next token can continue it. so if a line starts with *, ( or - it gets glued onto the previous line, same as js asi. "b = a" followed by a line with "-1" compiles fine and gives you b = a - 1. i listed the ones i know about in the readme.

normal c with semicolons still works and you can mix both. -run and shebangs work like in tcc. it can compile itself

demo page with a few examples: https://tanjim.org/slcc/demo.html

please don't use this for anything real

records.title: Show HN: Open-source customer-facing agents
records.author: zualas
records.storyText:
Hi, Dmitri from Radioso here, an open-source platform to design AI agents for customers and visitors in any channel, in the style of Fin/Ada/Decagon. The repo is https://github.com/radioso-ai/radioso and our website is https://radioso.ai

Today, your choices are:

1. Buy a very expensive service for your vertical (usually starting with $$ five figures monthly) 2. Get a cheap off-the-shelf chatbot that mostly answers FAQs 3. Build your own, and then also build the inbox, human handoff, audit trail and integrations around it

At Radioso we wanted an open-source option that combines the best of all 3. You can integrate it with your own software via API/SDK or your CRM, or run it standalone, either self-hosted or in our cloud.

The engine runs multi-step interactions and takes actions: calling your APIs, updating records, booking things. Maybe you’ve tried Parlant; Radioso is the alternative “with batteries included”: RAG, audit trail, customer service inbox, and integrations like Slack and email.

Under the hood it’s plain TypeScript + PostgreSQL, works with OpenAI/Anthropic/other models, and is licensed under Apache 2.0 which includes all features (The only thing we keep under EE license is the multi-tenant layer we use to run our own cloud).

We have existing customers running it for technical Q&A, course booking, online product recommendations and goods returns, among others, some reaching 92% of conversations automated. We’re currently working on voice support so we can offer a call center.

Our ambition is to be “the WordPress of customer-facing AI” :), where people can contribute their favorite plugins and benefit from the ecosystem.

Longer term, we think browsing the web will mostly mean talking to your own agent, and when you need a service or a purchase, your agent will talk to the vendor’s agent to get things done. For this, Radioso already publishes an A2A Agent Card and we’re working on the rest. Your Radioso services are also callable over MCP, for customers who already use it.

Thanks for your attention. We’d especially love to hear which integrations you’d want, whether you’d self-host it, and what’s stopped you from deploying a customer-facing AI agent so far. Tell us what you think.

records.title: Show HN: Control Layer Demo for AI Coding Agents
records.author: MintCoder
records.storyText:
Letting coding agents (such as Claude Code) work autonomously on repos on a daily-basis, brings a high level of uncertainty. For those who won't let the agent decide alone whether it can create/modify or delete any folder on their repos; I wanted to be able to trace actions performed and being able to let the agent continue his work autonomously, or ask him to request a human approval according to some criteria defined. 
After investigations, the cleanest way to do it was according to me to develop a deterministic control layer between the LLM and the work of the agent that would track and catch potential non-respect of pre-defined rules. 
How? by first setting up approval rules (Pass/requires approval/refused) before the work of the agent, and afterwards controlling cryptographic SHA 256 verifications, etc.
This allows to compare the before-after work of the agent.
I have put in my public GitHub repo a demo that you can launch easily and observe different scenarios behaviors like applied authorized modification, protected file waiting for Human approval, or outside perimeter authorization modification refused. The demo is offline, does not involve the official runtime, in native node.js and without dependencies. It should still allow you to understand the core principles.
I would like to know: how do you implement and handle safety boundaries? Especially if you let agents work on critical data/sensitive codebases? With which guardrails?

records.title: Show HN: emcee – macOS Stage Manager alternative
records.author: campfireshuffle
records.storyText:
I am one of the (dozens!) of users of Stage Manager, but I don't like some of its UX choices. For example, it moves newly opened windows into a new stage, which breaks my focus.

I spent some time trying to see if I could modify SkyLight and Window Manager to tweak Stage Manager behaviors, but this required me to turn off SIP and the experience was janky.

So I built a full replacement that still feels great to use. You can make as many stages as you want, reorder them, and drag windows and apps between them. IMO all the drag-and-drop behaviors work the way you’d expect.

Like several recent window managers, emcee hides windows in an invisible Space (I learned this from yabai), and it works with SIP on. There were lots of little edge cases to get right, e.g:

  - Keeping the strip’s previews fresh without hammering Screen Recording
  - Cmd-Tab switching to the right stage and putting focus somewhere sensible.
  - "Save dialogs", listening for app quit events, etc.
Happy to answer any questions!
